profile.summary: Ephesians presents Paul amazed at the saving grace of God in Christ and with the divine plan to form a new community in which Jews and Gentiles belong equally to the same people. The letter unites doctrine and practice: first celebrates what God did in Christ - election, adoption, forgiveness, seal of the Spirit, reconciliation and unity - and then calls believers to live worthy of this vocation, in humility, holiness, love, order in the home and spiritual vigilance. Writing of prison, the letter has a tone of joy, praise and gratitude, and offers one of the richest visions of Christian life in the New Testament.
profile.setting: The letter relates to the period of Paul's third missionary journey, with a strong connection to Ephesus, capital and large port of the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of present-day Turkey. Ephesus was a very influential and cosmopolitan city, marked by the movement of people and the presence of the famous temple of Artemis. Paul spent a long and difficult period there, facing opposition and suffering, while the gospel spread throughout the province, originating small groups of Christians in various cities and towns. As for authorship, tradition attributes the letter to Paul, but some scholars question this based on vocabulary, style and context; the introduction, however, argues that there is no decisive reason to deny Pauline authorship. As for the addressee, although traditionally linked to the church of Ephesus, the letter may have been a circular message for various churches in Asia. The date and location are also debated: it may have been written from Rome, around 60-62 AD, or from a prison in Ephesus, at an earlier date, about 53-56 AD.

structure.label: The grace of God in Christ
structure.description: Praise for God's salvation, including choice, forgiveness, adoption, seal of the Spirit, prayer for spiritual understanding and the remembrance that Jews and Gentiles were reconciled in Christ.

structure.label: The call to a dignified life
structure.description: Exhortation to unity, humility, grace and growth of the body of Christ, with the use of the gifts granted by God.

structure.label: New life and transformed relationships
structure.description: Called to abandon the old way of life, to walk as children of light and to reflect holiness, purity, gratitude and love. Relationships in the home must be shaped by respect and love in Christ.

structure.label: Spiritual conflict and conclusion
structure.description: Warning about the battle against the devil, with the need to depend on the armor God provides, followed by personal closure and final blessing.

themes: The sovereignty of God's grace in salvation
The unity between Jews and Gentiles in the church
Christian Life as a Practical Response to the Gospel
Holiness, love and gratitude in everyday life
Spiritual conflict and dependence on God's provision
readingKeys: Notice the sequence of the letter: first what God did for us, then how we should live in response.
Realize how Paul insists that Gentiles and Jews are fully equal in Christ, without second-class Christians.
Read the ethical advice not as isolated moralism, but as the fruit of the new identity received in Christ and the power of the Spirit.
profile.cautions: The Pauline authorship, the original recipient and the exact date are debated subjects; therefore, it is appropriate to deal with these issues with caution. The letter also presupposes strong ethnic tensions between Jews and Gentiles and a robust view of sin and judgment, which may sound hard on the modern reader, but it is central to the logic of the text. Finally, the section on spiritual warfare should be read in the tone of the letter: dependence on God and use of the protection it provides, not aggressive triumphalism.

dossier.narratedEra: The book depicts the world of early Christianity in the Roman province of Asia, with Ephesus as an urban and missionary center in the time of Paul's third missionary journey (c. A.D. 53,57), when the Christian community was still forming between Jews and Gentiles and under pressure from the Roman Empire. The letter also looks at the daily life of domestic churches in Asia Minor, ethnic tensions, and the reality of spiritual and social opposition.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes traditionally place the composition in the period when Paul was imprisoned. The traditional reading places it in Rome, in AD 60-62, or shortly before Paul's execution of AD 64-65; an alternative proposal, mentioned in the notes, was written in prison in Ephesus, which would place it earlier, around AD 53-56. The sources also record the debate about authorship: the traditional attribution is paulina, but some scholars propose a later disciple or an editor who reworked the letter.

politics.title: Ephesus as provincial capital and strategic imperial city
politics.detail: Ephesus is described as the capital and port city of the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of present-day Turkey, and as the fourth largest city in the Roman Empire, with population possibly around 500,000.
politics.readingImpact: This backdrop helps to read the letter as directed to a church in an urban, cosmopolitan and large circulation environment, in which the Christian mission reached an entire region, not just an isolated community.

politics.title: Persecution and opposition during ministry in Ephesus
politics.detail: The notes claim that during Paul's prolonged stay in Ephesus, he faced strong opposition and suffered much abuse, citing Acts 19:21-41 and Pauline references to prisons and sufferings.
politics.readingImpact: This illuminates the letter as a pastoral word born in the context of real conflict, which makes its themes of perseverance, God's power and less abstract and more urgent spiritual armor.

politics.title: Imperial power and superior authority of Christ
politics.detail: Ephesians 1:21-22 is read in the notes as the language of Christ's supremacy over all rival, human or spiritual power, and the image of the victorious king with enemies under the feet is presented as figurative of real dominion.
politics.readingImpact: In a world of empires and hierarchies, the letter shifts the reader's maximum allegiance to Christ, relativizing any earthly power and reinforcing that the church lives under another sovereignty.

politics.title: Social structure of home, family and slavery in the early Christian world
politics.detail: The notes preserve the traditional relationships of the home - husband/wife, parents/childs, gentlemen/slaves, but insist that these relationships must be shaped by Christ. In the case of slavery, the note explicitly states that Paul did not promote it, but taught how to live within it as a fact of that culture.
politics.readingImpact: Reading should consider that Paul speaks to a society with asymmetrical domestic orders; the text is not socially neutral, but reorients duties and attitudes under the lordship of Christ.

politics.title: Relationship between Jews and Gentiles in the Roman Environment
politics.detail: The notes insist that there were traditional ethnic tensions between Jews and Gentiles throughout the Roman world, and that in Ephesians Paul combats the perception of inferiority or distancing of the Gentiles from the Jewish Christians.
politics.readingImpact: The letter should be read as a response to a concrete community problem of inclusion and equality, not only as an abstract treatise on spiritual unity.

customs.title: Old letters with expanded greeting
customs.detail: In Eph 1:1-2, the notes say that Paul follows the normal standard of the ancient Greek letters - presentation of the sender and greetings - but the Christianizes in emphasizing divine calling, holiness of the recipients, and the blessing of grace and peace.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the introduction is not mere formality: it already announces sovereignty of God, the identity of the community and the devotional tone of the letter.

customs.title: Domestic churches and circulation of the letter
customs.detail: The notes suggest that the letter may have been a circular message to several churches in the province of Asia, and observe the absence of personal greetings as a relevant data for this hypothesis.
customs.readingImpact: This changes the reading of Ephesians of letter to a document-specific church with wider regional application, useful for diverse communities and perhaps with many new converts.

customs.title: Domestic life under Christian discipline
customs.detail: In Eph 6:1-4, the notes deal with the obedience of children and paternal discipline as an expression of devotion to the Lord, warning against the hardness and injustice of the parents.
customs.readingImpact: The home appears as a space of spiritual formation, and not only of authority; the exhortation corrects abuses and reorients education for good and for the Lord.

customs.title: Slavery as a present social fact, not Christian ideal
customs.detail: In Eph 6:5-9, the notes state that Paul is teaching how to live within slavery, and not endorsing the institution. Slaves are called to serve faithfully; the lords, to treat kindly, without threats and without favoritism.
customs.readingImpact: The text must be read within an existing social order, but morally criticized for reciprocal duties under the same heavenly Lord.

customs.title: Worship marked by praise, prayer and blessing
customs.detail: The notes highlight that Ephesians is full of gratitude, praise, prayer, and doxology; even writing from prison, the tone is of joy and thanksgiving, with blessings and prayers in 1:3-14; 1:15-23; 3:14-21; 6:21-24.
customs.readingImpact: The letter works as a piece of worship and formation, showing that the appropriate answer to grace is worship and gratitude, not just moral instruction.

language.title: "Mysterious plan as truth before hidden and now revealed
language.detail: The notes explain that the "mystery" in Paul is a divine truth previously hidden and now revealed in the gospel; in Ephesians, this mystery refers mainly to the inclusion of the Gentiles and the meeting of everything in Christ.
language.readingImpact: Helps to read the letter as a revelation of God's purpose in history, not as secret or enigmatic speculation.

language.title: A long and interconnected Greek phrase at 1:3-14
language.detail: The notes note that Eph 1:3-14 is a single complex sentence in Greek, among the longest of Paul's letters, reflecting the interconnection of ideas.
language.readingImpact: The reader must accompany the theological flow as a great explosion of praise, rather than artificially fragmenting the paragraph.

language.title: Vocabulary seal, warranty and inheritance
language.detail: In Eph. 1:13-14, the Spirit is described as a seal of possession and assurance of future blessings; in 1:11-18, inheritance, adoption and reliable hope appear.
language.readingImpact: These images give security to the community: belonging, future and identity have already been assured by God.

language.title: Image of head and body / fullness
language.detail: The notes understand the church as the body of Christ and see in 1:23 the idea that the church is the full expression of Christ in this world.
language.readingImpact: The metaphor is not only organizational; it defines the identity of the church as a visible extension of Christ's action.

language.title: Metaphor of Roman armor
language.detail: In Eph 6:14-17, the notes claim that Paul wears the armor of a Roman soldier as an image of the spiritual equipment; most of it is defensive, not offensive. The sword is the exception and represents the word of God.
language.readingImpact: The passage should be read as called to firmness and resistance, not to an offensive against the devil.

timeline.title: The third missionary journey of Paul with center in Ephesus
timeline.detail: The notes situate this period in AD 53-57, with Ephesus as the main center of operation.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone explains why the city and the province appear as the missionary horizon of the letter and why several churches in the region seem to be in the backdrop.

timeline.title: Extended stay in Ephesus after previous brief visit
timeline.detail: Paul would have made an initial brief visit, then returned to stay between two and three years in Ephesus, according to notes based on Acts 18:19-21 and 19:1-20:1.
timeline.readingImpact: The long coexistence makes Paul's familiarity plausible with the region and also the strangeness of the absence of personal greetings if the letter were only for Ephesus.

timeline.title: Conflicts and prisons associated with ministry in Ephesus
timeline.detail: The notes link the intense opposition in Ephesus to Paul's references on afflictions and prisons, especially 2 Cor 11:23-27 and 2 Cor 1:8-9; the letter presupposes a context of suffering.
timeline.readingImpact: This reinforces the reading of Ephesians as a letter written under real pressure, which explains the focus on perseverance, prayer and divine power.

timeline.title: Possible composition in Rome, AD 60'62, or just before AD 64-65
timeline.detail: The introduction says that Ephesians is traditionally understood as a letter from the written prison of Rome, placing it between AD 60 or just before Paul's death around AD 64-65.
timeline.readingImpact: If this chronology is followed, the letter belongs to the final period of Paul's activity and gains weight as a mature synthesis of the gospel.
timeline.reference: Introduction: Date and Place of Writing

timeline.title: Alternative composition proposal in prison in Ephesus, AD 53-56
timeline.detail: The notes also mention the hypothesis of writing in prison in Ephesus, which would shift the date to earlier, around AD 53-56.
timeline.readingImpact: This possibility brings the letter closer to the period of great activity in Ephesus and can explain its direct connection with the churches of Asia.
timeline.reference: Introduction: Date and Place of Writing

investigation: The Pauline tradition is affirmed, but the notes record academic debate about authorship by later disciple or later edition; the lexical, stylistic and theological analysis is presented as an argument of the debate, not as conclusive proof.

The hypothesis of circular letter is supported by the absence of 'emphesus' in ancient manuscripts and the lack of personal greetings; however, the traditional inscription to Ephesus is also preserved in Matthew Henry's notes.
The notes offer two compositional chronologies, Rome or Ephesus; there is no final decision in the sources provided.
The exact relationship between the churches of Asia, the origin of false perceptions of Gentiles and the process of circulation of the letter is mentioned as likely, but not clarified in the notes.
The references to 'Roman'ars and the domestic structure are interpretive contextualizations of the notes, not exhaustive descriptions of the old society.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the attached notes of Tyndale Open Study Notes and Matthew Henry. Therefore, it covers only what these sources really mention: Ephesus, Paul's mission, the debate on recipients, authorship and date, as well as explicitly commented on social and literary themes. There is no independent historical reconstruction, nor filling gaps with external data. Some topics appear selectively: for example, worship, family, slavery and spiritual warfare receive more attention because notes emphasize them, while other aspects of the daily life and imperial politics are only inferred from what the notes say. There is also unresolved controversy in the sources themselves: Pauline authorship is traditional and defended by the notes, but the hypothesis of a later disciple/editor is recognized; likewise, the composition in Rome and in Ephesus remain possibilities presented, not closed conclusions.
